en_alt: The arrow struck the target.
note: Accurate; 'struck' is an equally valid rendering of попа́ла.

en_alt: The team has five experienced marksmen.
note: Existential В кома́нде also renders naturally as 'The team has'.

en_alt: The medal was presented to the young marksman.
note: вручи́ть is specifically 'present/award'; keep 'given' but accept the closer verb.
With никогда́ Russian normally takes the imperfective (никогда́ не прома́хивался); the negated perfective reads oddly here.

en_alt: She has many noble aspirations.
note: све́тлый in this collocation is 'noble/high-minded'; 'bright aspirations' is the literal reading, kept as en_gb.

en_alt: His striving for knowledge is astonishing.
note: Equally valid rendering of стремле́ние к + удивля́ет.

en_alt: To paint the ceiling, a stepladder is needed.
note: The impersonal нужна́ also maps to a passive-style English without the added 'you'.

en_alt: He climbed onto the stepladder.
note: на + accusative is 'onto'; both readings are natural.

en: The city authorities are pleased about the new construction.
note: 'glad of the new construction' is not an English collocation; 'pleased about' keeps the dative sense.

ru: В э́той стране́ был друго́й строй.
note: The English 'system' is right for this (socio-political order) sense of строй, but the headword gloss 'formation' does not cover it — the gloss is probably the half that needs widening.

en_alt: The commander walked along the ranks.
note: 'ranks' is the usual English for a military строй.

en_alt: The soldiers got into formation.
note: в + accusative carries motion into formation, which the alt makes explicit.

en_alt: We are studying the structure of the cell.
note: Russian has no articles, so definite and indefinite readings are both valid.

en_alt: Changes have taken place in the structure of the firm.
note: Equally valid rendering of произошли́.

en_alt: The library issues textbooks to students free of charge.
note: выдава́ть is 'issue/give out' rather than 'lend'; the alt tracks it more closely.

en_alt: The students are sitting an exam.
note: BrE 'sitting an exam' is an equally natural rendering of imperfective сдаю́т.

ru: Профе́ссор попроси́л студе́нтов сдать рабо́ты во вто́рник.
Профе́ссор посове́товал студе́нтам прочита́ть э́ту статью́.

en_alt: This student studies at a university.
note: Article choice is free in the Russian.

ru: Ма́ленький зал был те́сно уста́влен сту́льями.
en: The small hall was tightly packed with chairs.
en_alt: The little hall was packed tight with chairs.
note: 'packed tight with' reads awkwardly in a written sentence; 'tightly packed with' is the standard adverb placement.

en_alt: A book is lying on the chair.
note: The alt keeps лежи́т visible instead of the existential 'there is'.

en_alt: He put the chair by the window.
note: поста́вить is plain 'put/stand'; both are natural.

en_alt: He came down the steps.
note: Equally natural rendering of спусти́лся.

en_alt: Careful, this step is slippery!
Be careful, this step is slippery.
note: Осторо́жно is equally 'be careful'.

en_alt: The stewardess brought the water.
note: Article choice is free in the Russian.

ru: Она́ рабо́тает стюарде́ссой в но́вой компа́нии.
en_alt: She works as a stewardess at a new company.
note: в + company renders as 'at' or 'in' in English.

ru: Я спроси́ла стюарде́ссу о вре́мени полёта.

en_alt: She brought back souvenirs from the journey.
From the journey she brought back souvenirs.
note: путеше́ствие is glossed 'journey'; the fronted word order is also valid.

en_alt: He applied to the court.
He took the matter to court.
note: 'went to court' is the idiomatic rendering; the literal обрати́ться 'apply to' is worth accepting too.

en_alt: The case was heard in court.
note: 'heard' is the standard English legal verb for рассмотре́ть де́ло.

en: The trial will begin tomorrow morning.
en_alt: The court hearing will begin tomorrow morning.
note: 'The court will begin' is not English; here суд is the trial/hearing — the headword gloss 'court' may need widening.

en_alt: Big vessels were standing in the harbour.
note: Imperfective стоя́ли also renders as a past continuous.

en_alt: The captain is steering the vessel into port.
note: Imperfective present also renders as the English progressive.

en_alt: I paid a big sum.
note: большо́й is glossed 'big'; both are natural.

en_alt: This sum is too big.
note: Article-free Russian; 'big' is the closer gloss of велика́.

en_alt: Mum cooked a tasty soup.
Mum made a tasty soup.
note: свари́ть is specifically 'cooked (by boiling)'; the simple past is as valid as the perfect here.

ru: До́ма нет хле́ба, схожу́ в супермарке́т.

en_alt: We bought groceries in the supermarket.
note: в maps to 'in' or 'at' here.

en_alt: The new supermarket opened recently.
note: Article choice is free in the Russian.

en_alt: The present is intended for the husband.
note: супру́г is specifically the husband; пода́рок is glossed 'present'.

en_alt: She came with her husband.
note: супру́г denotes the husband; both renderings are correct.

en_alt: Her husband works at a bank.
note: Same sense, more usual English word.

en_alt: The shop is open twenty-four hours a day.
The shop works round the clock.
note: Idiomatic rendering is right; the alts give the learner the literal 'a full day and night' reading.

en_alt: We travelled for more than twenty-four hours.
note: су́тки is a full 24-hour day, which the alt makes explicit.

en_alt: The train was two whole days late.
note: дво́е су́ток is two full 24-hour periods.

ru: В су́ти э́того вопро́са лежи́т противоре́чие.
note: The Russian collocation is лежа́ть в осно́ве, not лежа́ть в су́ти; a native phrasing would be «В осно́ве э́того вопро́са лежи́т противоре́чие» or «Суть э́того вопро́са — противоре́чие», but rewriting it would drop or move the headword, so this needs a human decision.

en_alt: Get to the heart of the matter.
Get to the point.
note: The literal en_gb is fine; the idiomatic alts stop the drill rejecting them.

en_alt: Explain the essence of the problem to me.
note: Both English word orders are natural.

ru: В его́ существова́нии никто́ не сомнева́лся.
en_alt: Nobody doubted its existence.
No one doubted his existence.
note: его́ is ambiguous between 'his' and 'its'; both readings should be accepted.

en_alt: The scientists proved the existence of the planet.
note: Article choice is free in the Russian.

ru: Никто́ не ве́рил в его́ существова́ние.
en_alt: No one believed in its existence.
Nobody believed in his existence.
note: его́ is ambiguous between 'his' and 'its'.

ru: В э́том и есть су́щность пробле́мы.
en_alt: This is precisely the essence of the problem.
note: The emphatic и is carried by 'precisely' in the alt.

en_alt: He did not understand the essence of the matter.
note: вопро́с is 'question' or 'matter' here; both are natural.

en_alt: The engineer drew the diagram.
note: Article choice is free in the Russian.

en_alt: Everything is clear on the diagram.
note: Both English word orders are natural.

en_alt: The teacher explained a new diagram.
note: Article choice is free in the Russian.

ru: В сча́стье мы забыва́ем о вре́мени.
en_alt: When we are happy we forget about time.
note: The literal en_gb is acceptable; the alt is how an English speaker would usually put it.

en_alt: Bring the bill, please.
note: Both placements of 'please' are natural.

en_alt: We asked for two separate bills.
note: Common real-world reading of два счёта in a restaurant.

en_alt: The aeroplane is flying to the USA.
note: самолёт is glossed 'aeroplane'.

en_alt: The US president gave a speech.
note: Equally valid rendering of the genitive attribute.

en_alt: The party congress was held in the capital.
note: Equally natural rendering of прошёл.

ru: О реше́ниях съе́зда написа́ли в газе́тах.
en_alt: The newspapers wrote about the decisions of the congress.
note: The Russian is an impersonal plural; the active alt is the more usual English.

ru: По воскресе́ньям оте́ц хо́дит на рыба́лку с сыновья́ми.

en_alt: The mother allows her son to go out for a walk.
The mother lets her son go out.
note: гуля́ть is specifically going out for a walk / playing outside.

ru: Оте́ц с де́тства привива́л сыновья́м любо́вь к спо́рту.

en_alt: Their son studies at the university.
note: Article choice is free in the Russian.

en: He asked for more curd fritters.
en_alt: He asked for more syrniki.
note: The English left the word untranslated as 'syrniki' while the headword gloss (and the tap-hint) says 'curd fritter'; the transliteration is kept as an alt.

en: For breakfast we ate curd fritters.
en_alt: For breakfast we ate syrniki.
note: Same untranslated 'syrniki' against the 'curd fritter' gloss.

en_alt: He ate one syrnik.
note: Same untranslated 'syrnik' against the 'curd fritter' gloss.

en_alt: How may I help you, sir?
What can I help you with, sir?
note: Idiomatic and correct; the alts cover the usual variants.

'the sir' is not English — 'sir' is a vocative or a title before a name; the sentence would need the Russian changed (e.g. «Слуга́ поклони́лся сэ́ру Джо́ну.» → 'The servant bowed to Sir John'), which touches the dative slot, so it needs a human decision.

en_alt: We drove through the thick taiga.
We travelled through the thick taiga.
note: густо́й is glossed 'thick'; е́хать is by vehicle.

en_alt: Scientists have uncovered many secrets of nature.
note: раскры́ть is equally 'uncover'; the perfect is as valid as the simple past.

en_alt: This will stay a secret between us.
note: оста́ться is glossed 'to stay'.

en_alt: She is keeping a big secret.
note: Imperfective present also renders as the English progressive.

ru: Такси́ст бы́стро довёз нас до до́ма.
en_alt: The taxi driver quickly drove us home.
note: довёз is specifically 'drove/took by vehicle as far as'.

en_alt: He works as a taxi driver at nights.
note: по ноча́м is habitual plural; both English forms are natural.

en_alt: I paid the taxi driver for the ride.
note: пое́здка is equally 'ride' in this context.

en_alt: She has a big talent.
She has great talent.
note: большо́й is glossed 'big'; English also drops the article here.

en_alt: There are many young talents in the school.
note: в шко́ле renders as 'in' or 'at' the school.

en_alt: He has a talent.
note: облада́ть is 'possess'; the plainer verb is equally valid English.

en_alt: There were many dances at the party.
There were a lot of dances at the celebration.
note: пра́здник covers 'party'/'celebration'/'holiday'; мно́го is glossed 'a lot'.

en_alt: She learnt a new dance.
note: 'learnt' is the BrE spelling and should not be marked wrong.

en_alt: My slippers are standing by the door.
note: стоя́т is 'are standing'; en_gb's plainer 'are' is the more natural English.

en_alt: Put your slippers on, the floor is cold.
note: English usually supplies the possessive here.

en_alt: There are a lot of clean plates in the cupboard.
note: мно́го is glossed 'a lot'.

en_alt: There is an empty plate on the table.
note: Both English word orders render the Russian's fronted locative.

en_alt: There is a lot of light in his work.
note: мно́го is glossed 'a lot'; тво́рчество here is the body of work.
The English 'creative work' (the poet's oeuvre) is the right sense, but the headword gloss 'creativity' does not cover it — the gloss looks like the half that needs widening.

en_alt: She is keen on folk arts and crafts.
note: наро́дное тво́рчество is idiomatically 'folk art'; the alt covers the wider usual English.

ru: В моско́вских теа́трах биле́ты раскупа́ют за ме́сяц.
en_alt: In Moscow theatres tickets are bought up a month in advance.
note: The alt keeps раскупа́ют 'buy up' and the impersonal plural visible.

ru: Мы говори́ли о теа́тре весь ве́чер.
en_alt: We spoke about the theatre all evening.
note: говори́ть is glossed 'to speak'.

ru: В э́том те́ксте мно́го но́вых слов.
en_alt: There are a lot of new words in this text.
note: мно́го is glossed 'a lot'.

ru: Прочита́йте текст и отве́тьте на вопро́сы.

en_alt: She sent a telegram to her grandmother.
note: Both English complement orders are natural.

ru: В телегра́мме бы́ло то́лько два сло́ва.
en_alt: The telegram had only two words in it.
note: Alternative rendering of the fronted locative.
